@@53628644 <h> Mother Nature 's acid trip <p> There 's no more colourful display of the miracle of life than to slip on a snorkelling mask and dip your face into the warm water above a tropical reef . You 're tempted to lift your head back to the silver surface just to repeat the experience of dropping in on Mother Nature 's acid trip . <p> We are such land-bound animals that most of us do n't give enough thought to the sea . But the oceans have absorbed 90 per cent of the heat we 've generated by spewing fossil carbon into the sky . And they 're paying the price . <p> The oceans are getting hotter , acidifying , and suffering prolonged heat waves . You have probably heard about mass bleaching events , most famously on the Great Barrier Reef , when marine heat waves kill off coral . <p> Just like on land , heat waves in the sea are ever more intense and frequent . And they can spread across truly vast areas . One marine heat wave in 2015-16 caused mass bleaching of corals across the Pacific , Atlantic and Indian oceans @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ without coral reefs is closer than we 'd realized . <p> " At 1.5 C of warming , which the world is predicted to reach in the early 2030s without drastic action to limit greenhouse gas emissions , 99 per cent of the world 's reefs will experience heat waves that are too frequent for them to recover . " <p> That 99 per cent is not a typo . And wealthy scuba tourists are not the concern . A billion people in the global tropics rely on reefs for food and livelihoods . @@53628876 <p> Like so many conversations in this era , my talk with former Bank of Canada governor Stephen Poloz happened on a Zoom call . Mostly , we discussed his upcoming book , The Next Age of Uncertainty , a primer on the economic volatility ahead . That 's where I first broached the idea that longer-term trends could interact and cause unpredictable outcomes . <h> Q : You do n't see a lot of macroeconomics books targeting a household audience , a government audience and a business audience all at once . What are the big issues they 're thinking about that could affect those decisions over a five- or 10-year horizon ? Which we hardly ever think about , but it matters . <h> Q : You point to a number of " tectonic forces " -- population aging , technological progress , growing inequality and climate change -- and argue they will cause greater uncertainty and volatility overall . <p> A : With businesses , there 's such a complex planning environment . They will claim to their board that they 're looking at the long term , and if the world turns out really badly , this is what it 's going to look like . Or if the world turns out really good . But I think they spend less time than they should exploring what they will do when those good or bad things happen , because they 're more likely now . <h> Q : You explain this as if a bell curve is becoming more of a straight line . <p> A : What you think of as your main scenario @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many more possibilities spread out there . It 's like when the Ferrari of athletes gets a cold . It lasts two days because they 're in such great condition . You can see the differences around the world . Economies that were n't in that situation suffered more . The second important lesson was fiscal policy like CERB can do a really good job of stabilizing the economy . They played a really important stabilizing role . <h> Q : What are your @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ politics right now ? <p> A : It runs the gamut from plain wrong to just unthoughtful . @@53629290 <p> Over the past two years , charitable organizations in Canada have been battered by the fierce tides of a global pandemic , struggling to stay afloat while still serving their communities . <p> The turmoil has been destabilizing , but it 's also proved to be a catalyst by provoking serious conversations about the future of a vibrant sector , which , in one form or another , has sustained and expanded our Canadian social fabric . <p> The sector has expanded rapidly in recent years , and responded to growth in both diversity and needs . There are now more than 170,000 charitable and non-profit organizations employing two million people in every region of the country and contributing more than eight per cent of Canada 's total GDP -- more than the retail sector and almost as much as the oil and gas industry . <p> Despite the best efforts of employees and volunteers from charitable and non-profit organizations across the country , these ties that bind us are fraying from polarization and crisis after crisis , including : the pandemic , #MeToo and its aftermath , the impact of Black Lives Matter , the discovery of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the growing effects of climate change , and rapidly increasing income inequalities . <p> These events have contributed to the rise of the social unrest we 're seeing . They signal the end of business as usual for every government and organization , and our sector is n't just bracing for change , we 're embracing it . As we 're on the front lines , we 've been seeing and living these truths as they grow in the public consciousness . <p> But to rebuild a more resilient and inclusive country , the charitable and non-profit sector needs more attention and a more effective partnership with the federal government . <p> An encouraging step in this direction is the Senate 's Bill S-216 to amend the Income Tax Act , known as the Effective and Accountable Charities Act , which just passed first reading in the House of Commons . <p> The current Income Tax Act stipulates that charities must spend their dollars only on their " own activities . " This requirement has been described as both outdated and colonial , because it prevents charities from partnering @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Indigenous communities , and civil-society groups -- vital social-good organizations without charitable status , otherwise known as non-qualified donees . <p> These non-qualified donees often comprise traditionally marginalized or racialized communities that provide unparalleled grassroots knowledge , networks , and expertise , but , for a range of real and legitimate reasons , are not charities . <p> The changes proposed in this non-partisan bill -- which was adopted unanimously by the Senate , tabled by Conservative MP Philip Lawrence , and seconded by NDP MP Heather McPherson -- would allow charities , especially foundations ( a type of charity that usually makes grants to other charities ) , to collaborate in truer partnerships with these groups . <p> They would amplify the voices of marginalized communities at this critical moment in history . They 'd also increase their access to valuable resources while safeguarding accountability and transparency . It 's a simple administrative change that could transform the charitable sector by making it more inclusive and reflective of the communities we serve . <p> Of course , this is n't a silver bullet . Most financial contributions to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but from government and individual donors . It 's clear , however , that new operating models and forward-thinking policies and programs are needed to support the critical work of our sector in this ever-changing and increasingly complex world . <p> We need to work together in partnership with the government to develop new and better ways to get more resources into communities where they 're needed most , now and in the future . There are several ways to increase resources for our sector for the long term and to amplify their impact , from a sustainable increase in the disbursement quota , to creative ways to expand impact investing , to simple changes to the way data about our sector is collected and evaluated . <p> The path forward is n't without challenges , including a shrinking donor base , an aging population , the volatile job market , and rising inflation . But the opportunities are bright , and there are several areas where our sector can immediately contribute valuable knowledge and advice . The charitable and non-profit sector has first-hand , on-the-ground experience in every community @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shape concrete and productive forward movement . <p> We 're committed to positive change that leaves no one behind , and we can do that far more effectively if we can work more formally and collaboratively with the federal government , MPs , and senators to build and maintain policy and programs that serve all residents of this country -- and , despite the tensions and challenges afflicting our country , strengthen the common good . We look forward to having that opportunity . <p> Jean-Marc Mangin is president of Philanthropic Foundations Canada , a national network of family , independent , and corporate grant-makers in Canada that includes many of the largest private charitable foundations in the country . <p> The views , opinions and positions expressed by all iPolitics columnists and contributors are the author 's alone . @@53629357 <h> Just 16% of the world 's coastlines are in good shape -- and many are so bad they can never fully recover <p> Only about 16% of the world 's coastal regions are in relatively good condition , according to our world-first research released today , and many are so degraded they ca n't be restored to their original state . ( Pixabay photo ) <p> Only about 16% of the world 's coastal regions are in relatively good condition , according to our world-first research released today , and many are so degraded they ca n't be restored to their original state . <p> Places where the land meets the sea are crucial for our planet to function . They support biodiversity and the livelihoods of billions of people . But to date , understanding of the overall state of Earth 's coastal regions has been poor . <p> Our research , involving an international team of experts , revealed an alarming story . Humanity is putting heavy pressure on almost half the world 's coastal regions , including a large proportion of protected areas . <p> All nations must ramp up efforts to preserve and restore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ right now . <p> Many animal species , including those that migrate , rely on coastlines for breeding , foraging and protection . Coastal sites are also where rivers discharge , mangrove forests exchange nutrients with the ocean , and tidal flows are maintained . <p> Humans also need coastlines . Among other functions , they support our fisheries , protect us from storms and , importantly , store carbon to help mitigate climate change . <p> As much as 74% of the world 's population live within 50 kilometres of the coast , and humans put pressure on coastal environments in myriad ways . <p> cropping and pasture lands , which clears ecosystems and causes chemical and nutrient runoff into waterways . <p> To date , assessments of the world 's coastal regions have largely focused solely on either the land or ocean , rather than considering both realms together . Our research sought to address this . <h> A troubling picture <p> We integrated existing human impact maps for both land and ocean areas . This enabled us to assess the spectrum of human pressure across Earth 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ those intact . <p> Both maps use data up to the year 2013 -- the most recent year for which cohesive data is available . <p> No coastal region was free from human influence . However , 15.5% of Earth 's coastal regions remained intact -- in other words , humans had exerted only low pressure . Many of the intact coastal regions were in Canada , followed by Russia and Greenland . <p> Large expanses of intact coast were also found elsewhere including Australia , Indonesia , Papua New Guinea , Chile , Brazil and the United States . <p> Troublingly , 47.9% of coastal regions have been exposed to very high levels of human pressure . And for 84% of countries , more than half their coastal regions were degraded . <p> What 's more , human pressures were high in about 43% of protected coastal regions -- those regions purportedly managed to conserve nature . <p> Coastal regions containing sea grasses , savannah and coral reefs had the highest levels of human pressure compared to other coastal ecosystems . Some coastal regions may be so degraded they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and once lost , it is likely impossible to restore them to their original state . <h> So where to now ? <p> It 's safe to say intact coastal regions are now rare . We urge governments to urgently conserve the coastal regions that remain in good condition , while restoring those that are degraded but can still be fixed . <p> To assist with this global task , we have made our dataset publicly available and free to use here . <p> Of course , the right conservation and restoration actions will vary from place to place . The actions might include , but are not limited to : <p> improving environmental governance and laws related to encroaching development <p> increasing well-resourced protected areas <p> mitigating land-use change to prevent increased pollution run-off <p> better community and local engagement <p> strengthening Indigenous involvement in managing coastal regions <p> effective management of fishing resources <p> addressing climate change <p> tackling geopolitical and socioeconomic drivers of damage to coastal environments . <p> In addition , there 's an urgent need for national and global policies and programs to effectively managing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's impact on Earth 's coastal regions is already severe and widespread . Without urgent change , the implications for both coastal biodiversity and society will become even more profound .

@@53629792 <h> Native birds have vanished across the continent since colonisation . Now we know just how much we 've lost <p> To give birds and other animals a chance at survival , we need effective national leadership not only to protect existing habitats , but also to restore lost habitat and manage future habitat under climate change . ( Pixabay photo ) <p> In the 250 years since Europeans colonised Australia , native birdlife has disappeared across the continent . Our new research has , for the first time , registered just how much Australia has actually lost -- and our findings are astonishingly sad . <p> We focused on 72 species of birds faced with extinction today , including the Kangaroo Island glossy black cockatoo , regent honeyeater , and night parrot . We found 530 million hectares , or 69% , of Australia , has lost at least one bird species . In some parts of the country , we 've lost up to 17 birds . <p> Land clearing , along with threats such as cat predation , have driven ten birds to disappear from over 99% of their historical habitat . Indeed , we show @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hectares of now-threatened bird habitat cleared on mainland Australia -- that 's 15% of Australia 's landmass . <p> For many of the species we examined , their remaining habitats occur in patches surrounded by farmland , towns and cities . To give birds and other animals a chance at survival , we need effective national leadership not only to protect existing habitats , but also to restore lost habitat and manage future habitat under climate change . <h> Lost , but not forgotten <p> In the last 250 years , 22 native birds have gone extinct . We found two more currently listed as threatened under Australia 's environmental legislation may also be now extinct . <p> One is the eastern star finch . This bird was once found from northern New South Wales to Queensland 's Burdekin River . A victim of overgrazing , it has not been seen since 1995 . Surprisingly , this bird is only listed as " endangered " rather than " critically endangered " under Australian law <p> The other is the Tiwi Islands hooded robin , which has not been seen for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ invasive species such as cats and weeds have likely driven it to extinction . <p> Other species are on their last legs . The western ground parrot , for example , once swept across large parts of Western Australia , but are now in just two locations : Cape Arid National Park and Nuytsland Nature Reserve . <p> They 've become locally extinct across more than 99% of their historical habitat because of habitat destruction , invasive species , and changed fire patterns . They 're at significant risk from isolated catastrophic events such as major bushfires . For example , the 2019-2020 fires alone destroyed 40% of the bird 's last remaining habitat . <p> The plight of the regent honeyeater is another tragic story of decline . Flocks of thousands once occurred from Adelaide to north of Brisbane , with the naturalist John Gould writing in 1865 : <p> I met with it in great abundance among the brushes of New South Wales ... I have occasionally seen flocks of from fifty to a hundred in numbers , passing from tree to tree as if engaged in a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , or in search of a more abundant supply of food . <p> Today , only 100 breeding pairs are left , and almost all breed in just three sites in NSW . The species has lost more than 86% of its historical habitat , with land clearing the main driver of decline . So few remain that young birds can not learn to sing properly , so have trouble attracting a mate . <h> The extinction wave <p> Our research used a combination of historical field guides , reference books , research papers , government records , spatial data , and expert elicitation to create maps of past habitats , and compared those to current habitats . <p> We found certain areas across continental mainland Australia to be in worse shape than others . <p> For example , we revealed extinction hotspots in areas between Swan Hill in Victoria and Marmon Jabuk range in South Australia . In this region , up to 17 birds have gone extinct ( red areas in map ) , such as the black-eared miner . <p> Likewise , over the last century , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in SA 's Mount Lofty ranges . This includes the rufous fieldwren , bush stone-curlew , ground parrot , king quail , azure kingfisher , barking owl , regent honeyeater , and swift parrot . <p> The story of decline is not limited to only threatened species , with more common birds such as willie wagtails , brolgas , boobook owls , and even magpies now disappearing from many places they were once common . <p> Indeed , the loss of so many species is the canary in the coal mine of total ecosystem collapse . And total ecosystem collapse poses an existential threat to food systems , water quality and climate stability . <p> If we do n't make fundamental changes in the way we manage and use landscapes , the extinction wave will continue to inundate Australia . <h> What can we do about it ? <p> We need federal leadership to curb the extinction crisis , and an important start is to implement promises we 've already signed up to in , for example , the UN 's Aichi biodiversity targets . <p> At the ongoing international @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ countries to halt human-induced species extinctions from now onwards , to bring the overall risk of species extinctions to zero , and to bring population abundance of native species back to 1970s levels by 2050 . This is a basic commitment to Australia 's heritage and culture . <p> These standards must be put in place as a matter of urgency . They must be legally enforceable , concise , specific , and focused on the conservation outcomes to properly protect Australian biodiversity and reverse the decline of our iconic places .

( Full disclosure : I called it that too , and I stand by my opinion that it was pivotal . ) <p> There 's nothing wrong with this rhetorical flourish ; it 's hard to overstate the importance or urgency of acting on climate change . But here 's the truth : no single year is make-or-break for climate policy . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a lifelong lab . Most of the time , policy change happens in a series of small improvements : this piece of policy is tweaked , public opinion on climate shifts a few points . And these small wins add up . <p> Then sometimes , there are big years , and 2022 could be one of them for Canada . <p> One such watershed moment will happen soon . By the end of March , we can expect to see Canada 's first emissions reduction plan , as required by the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act . New environment minister Steven Guilbeault has a challenge on his hands , as the country needs a robust plan to achieve the federal target of 40 to 45 per cent reductions by 2030 . To deliver on this goal , the plan will need to be comprehensive , provide clear signals to all sectors and set up actions consistent with the deep reductions needed to reach net zero by 2050 . <p> However robust our plan to reduce emissions , Canada also needs to prepare for the effects of climate change that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ twice as quickly as the global average , and figuring out how to protect ourselves from climate extremes shot up to near the top of the federal government 's to-do list after the B.C. heatwaves and floods in 2021 . The country 's first National Adaptation Strategy will be published this fall , and will need to both identify adaptation needs and develop actionable policies to boost Canada 's climate resilience . <p> Along with this marquee piece of policy , 2022 should also see measures tackling immediate adaptation priorities across governments , like up-to-date , accessible data on climate-related risks such as flooding ; faster building code updates ; and investments to protect the most vulnerable . <p> As global markets come to grips with the transformation required to tackled climate change , Canada has some catch-up to do in terms of climate-related financial disclosures -- the regulations that require companies to disclose how the net-zero transition and the effects of climate change could affect their future profitability . These rule changes , an essential element of the broader push to build a low-carbon , resilient economy , is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that could bring in some major shifts , it 's important to remember that policies are about real people : people 's health and well-being , livelihoods , homes and hopes for the future . The federal government continues to consult on how to ensure our economy thrives in the new net-zero transition , and 2022 should see concrete just-transition plans at the provincial and federal levels that could provide real supports and resources to affected workers and communities . <p> No doubt 2022 has a few surprises in store for us . Most of the respondents live and work in the Lower Mainland or on Vancouver Island , with only five per cent from the northeast and four per cent out of province . @@88746210 <p> " Consumers need to know that less and less of the money they spend on food actually makes it back to the farmer , " said National Farmers Union Vice-President of Operation and Saskatchewan farmer , Stewart Wells , in a recent media release . <p> In 2022 , it 's expected that people in Canada will pay between 5 and 7 per cent more for groceries , an increase of close to $1,000 a year for a family of four . <p> That is a noticeably high increase which will hit many families , lower-income earners , and those on fixed incomes hard . <p> This increase follows a similar increase in 2021 , which saw a family of four in Canada paying close to $700 more that year for food , an increase of 4 per cent overall . <p> The reasons for the food cost increases are likely not news for most readers . We have long heard , since the beginning of the pandemic , about transportation issues , supply chain disruptions , labour market shortages , high inflation , and now issues related to climate change . <p> In the 12th edition of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the estimated increases are detailed by food category . Compiled by Dalhousie University , Guelph University and this year for the first time the universities of Saskatchewan and British Columbia , the report assesses trends , costs , and impacts across the sector . The report also includes forecasts by province . And the report can be trusted , having accurately predicted food price increases in ten of the last 11 years . <p> Since 2020 of course the report has factored in the impact of COVID-19 on food prices and food insecurity . But the reality is that even before this pandemic , food prices in Canada increased by 70 per cent between 2000 and 2020 . Tally that up in terms of annual averages and food prices in this country during the same period rose between 6 to 7 per cent every year . And while for a time people in Canada spent a stable 10 per cent of their income on food , that percentage has been growing . Between 2015 and 2019 , the median income grew by 6.6 per cent . Meanwhile , food @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cent . <p> In 2019 , when food expenditures were measured by the Global Food Security Index , Canada ranked 18th . Canada now ranks 24th in the world . With near stagnant wages , people in Canada can expect a larger share of their income to be spent on food going forward . And , as noted , those earning the least will be the most affected by food price increases , as will people living in more remote communities , such as northern Canada . <p> Meanwhile , what the report does not measure in any way , is how this food inflation is impacted by the price that farmers receive at the farmgate for everything from wheat for flour to pork or beef . <p> So how are our family farmers doing ? Have the price of their products added to these price increases ? <p> The National Farmers Union ( NFU ) recently released information showing that food price increases can not be attributed to either the pandemic or to increases in prices paid to farmers . The information released by the NFU includes several telling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , pork , and other meat products . The charts are telling . <p> " Consumers need to know that less and less of the money they spend on food actually makes it back to the farmer , " said NFU Vice-President of Operation and Saskatchewan farmer , Stewart Wells , in a recent media release . " Retail food prices are high because meat packers , other large processors , and big retailers are taking ever larger shares . For most food products , the farmers ' share continues to shrink . " <p> This graph shows wheat and bread prices ( Stats Can and Gov't of Sask . ) It reveals that wheat prices are not the cause of bread price increases . But the graph hides a more striking fact : through most of the 1980s , Canada still had a two-price wheat policy . While the graph shows that in the 1980s farmers were receiving about $5 per bushel for their wheat -- a blended price representing export and domestic sales -- Canadian millers and bakers were paying about $7 per bushel of wheat they made @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , millers , bakers , and retailers were turning $7 per bushel wheat into $1 per loaf bread . In recent years , they 've been turning $7 wheat into $2.75 bread . The farmers ' share is about a third of what it was 40 years ago . <p> So then , the rise in food prices can not be attributed to increases in grain or livestock prices , supply issues , or COVID-19 , he noted . <p> If you consider the food price trends outlined in Canada 's Food Price Report 2022 and the information provided by the NFU relative to farm incomes , the picture becomes clearer . <p> Now compare these price increases to what has been happening with Canadian CEOs during this pandemic . <p> The report 's author , David Macdonald , writes , " The year 2020 might have been a bad one thanks to the COVID-19 pandemic , but for top CEO pay in Canada , it was another year in paradise . @@53636331 <h> Freedom Convoy raises questions for us all about law and order <p> ' This moment challenges activists and politicians across the political spectrum ; the issues to be confronted are n't exclusively the concerns of right-wing or left-wing partisans and sympathizers . ' <p> Senators and MPs who form the Parliamentary Black Caucus issued a statement Friday urging legislation to make it illegal to display the Confederate flag , such as the one waved by a Freedom Convoy protester on Parliament Hill on Jan. 29 , and other hate symbols , such as the Nazi swastika . ( Photo courtesy of Randy Boswell ) <p> The 12-day-long " Freedom Convoy " drama still unfolding in the heart of Canada 's capital raises a host of difficult questions about the right to protest in a democratic country -- and what the limits should be on demonstrations , marches , occupations , blockades , and acts of civil disobedience aimed at influencing public policy and driving social change . <p> This moment challenges activists and politicians across the political spectrum ; the issues to be confronted are n't exclusively the concerns of right-wing or left-wing partisans and sympathizers . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ expense -- should be tolerated to uphold the sacred freedoms of expression , assembly , and dissent ? When exactly does a legitimate -- even vital -- push against a perceived injustice cross the line into intimidation , trespassing , and vandalism , or more serious forms of criminality such as sabotage , assault , and sedition ? <p> And what if the purpose of a protest is so contentious , as it often is , that the goals of the protesters -- no matter how just they believe their cause to be -- deeply divide public opinion ? Should the degree of a protest 's popularity determine how hard protesters are allowed to push ? <p> Another dilemma : What if yesterday 's fringe viewpoint becomes tomorrow 's orthodoxy ? Does that retroactively justify past protest violence and other law-breaking actions ? How should we feel about criminal acts perpetrated , say , by anti-apartheid protesters in South Africa in the early 1980s when their eventual achievement represents one of history 's greatest human-rights triumphs ? <p> As critics debate how police and other authorities have managed ( or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's tempting for political progressives to condemn everything about this reactionary protest-cum-occupation against vaccine mandates : its anti-science impetus ; its absolutist embrace of individual rights over collective well-being ; its preposterous demand that all COVID-19 restrictions be ended or the federal Liberal government be overthrown ; its aggressive , overwrought takeover of downtown Ottawa ; its spawning of racist displays and other anti-social outrages . <p> But critics of this protest and its handling by police and government should , in fairness , acknowledge that envelope-pushing protesters in Canada are often champions of Indigenous rights , environmental protection , economic justice , and racial equality . <p> Comparisons and contrasts are already being widely discussed . <p> Some observers have argued that police in Ottawa have not cracked down on the trucker-led Freedom Convoy with the kind of authoritarian ferocity they 've routinely used against Indigenous protesters and environmental activists in the past . Why , they ask , have transport-truck blockades been tolerated on the doorstep of Parliament , at the Canada-U.S. border in Coutts , Alta. , and on the Ambassador Bridge connecting Detroit to Windsor , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ social-justice advocates have so often been confronted by battalions of police clad in riot gear ? <p> " If the blockade in Coutts consisted of Indigenous people , there would have been arrests and charges laid , " the leaders of Alberta 's Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation said in a statement issued last week . " Instead , the Coutts blockade is being allowed to continue , even though it has at times become violent . " <p> However , it must also be acknowledged that governments and law-enforcement agencies across Canada have increasingly favoured a kid-gloved de-escalation approach to a wide range of demonstrations that 's meant to defuse potentially explosive protests and avoid bloody clashes . <p> The 2020 rail blockades set up in various Canadian locations in solidarity with Indigenous opponents of a B.C. pipeline were not , in most cases , immediately dismantled with demonstrators hauled off to jail . But those protests -- lasting weeks , in some cases , and prompting prolonged negotiations -- did prompt Alberta 's United Conservative Party government to pass the Critical Infrastructure Defence Act , which gave police more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from damage or interference caused by blockades , protests , or similar activities . " <p> The same 2020 protests led federal Conservatives to condemn Prime Minister Justin Trudeau for preferring a brokered solution , described by then-Tory leader Andrew Scheer as " the weakest response to a national crisis in Canadian history . " <p> It 's also true that , for example , police waited more than five weeks in the fall of 2011 to end the left-wing Occupy Ottawa encampment in Confederation Park -- the same public space where Freedom Convoy protesters , to widespread dismay , built a shack , set up a kitchen , and stored propane tanks and other fuel canisters in recent days . <p> On the other hand , a " Defund Police " protest led by Black and Indigenous activists that blocked a major Ottawa intersection for 36 hours in November 2020 was brought to a swift and unexpected end in a 3 a.m. police raid that led to 12 arrests . Those protesters , who 'd been promised a meeting to negotiate with police board members the following day , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ officials and armed police " in the dead of night . " <p> None of these cases can be exactly compared to the Freedom Convoy , given its scale , outrageous aims , and murky funding arrangements . But we do need to consider what 's happening right now on and around Parliament Hill in the context of such previous protest movements as : Idle No More and Black Lives Matter ; other high-profile flash points such as Wet'suwet'en , Fairy Creek , Clayoquot Sound , Temagami , Ipperwash , and Oka ; and the protester-police showdowns at the APEC summit in Vancouver in 1997 and the G20 gathering in Toronto in 2010 . <p> Will the rules of engagement for police and demonstrators in future protests -- no matter the issue or political stripe of participants -- reflect lessons from the Freedom Convoy ordeal ? Will there be zero tolerance for the unruly behaviour that has frequently accompanied political protest in the past ? <p> The challenges posed by the trucker-led occupation of Ottawa could influence attitudes to other protest-related controversies in the news lately : the toppling of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were meant to end the public veneration of historical figures implicated in Canada 's residential-schools tragedy ; the harassing of health-care workers at anti-vaccination rallies held outside Canadian hospitals over the past year , prompting Trudeau 's election-campaign promise to introduce legislation banning such protests ; and even the unlawful unfurling of a Greenpeace anti-oil banner on the CN Tower in 2001 -- " CANADA AND BUSH CLIMATE KILLERS " -- by none other than Canada 's recently appointed federal Environment Minister Steven Guilbeault . <p> Finally , some of the disturbing ideas underlying the Freedom Convoy -- along with its controversial financing and forcefulness -- invite comparisons with the assault on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6 , 2021 , which some say inspired the Canadian truckers ' siege of Parliament Hill . <p> Decried by Democrats as nothing less than an " insurrection , " last year 's Capitol riot in Washington was downplayed in a resolution passed just a few days ago by the Republican National Committee as " ordinary citizens engaged in legitimate political discourse . " <p> To help clarify the many questions about balancing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has provoked , here 's a list of 10 issues -- there are more , of course -- that Canada 's lawmakers , policy analysts , and all citizens should contemplate : <p> The right to protest : Let 's acknowledge that the country should absolutely safeguard the freedom of Canadians to pick up placards , march to high-profile public places , and try to persuade fellow citizens and the country 's political leaders to pursue certain policies . Peaceful protest is at the heart of our democracy . <p> The disruption threshold : What complicates things is when a peaceful protest transforms into something else : an occupation or blockade that seriously disrupts economic activity , transportation routes , or the daily lives of significant numbers of ordinary citizens . This is why the residents and business owners of downtown Ottawa have appealed for relief from the Freedom Convoy 's thrall , even launching a class-action lawsuit . And it 's why the Indigenous blockades of key freight- and passenger-rail corridors in 2020 created enormous pressure to resolve the conflict to prevent hundreds of job losses and colossal commercial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ become unreasonable ? <p> Merits of the cause : Yes , whether the goals of a protest meet the test of worthiness is an eye-of-the-beholder judgment , and should always be subject to vigorous debate . In this country , in the 21st century , in light of growing awareness of historical injustices , it 's hard to condemn Indigenous protests or anti-racism rallies . Meanwhile , no objective observer would conclude that the Freedom Convoy 's stated goal of toppling Canada 's elected government -- if it does n't immediately implement the protesters ' demands to scrap all COVID restrictions -- is laughable and easily dismissed . But the merits of a vaccine mandate for cross-border truckers , the issue that sparked the convoy , is a reasonably debatable subject . <p> The de-escalation default : It 's clear that , in the case of the Freedom Convoy , and in many other occupation-type protests in recent years , police and political officials have taken a non-confrontational approach to ending the standoff . Some see this as coddling law-breakers or a form of " appeasement , " while others @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and bloodshed that could accompany a police raid or " bringing in the army , " as some impatient observers invariably demand . De-escalation typically involves " waiting out " the protesters , engaging in calm discussions over days or weeks , and letting exhaustion and cold , wet weather ( this is Canada , after all ) sap the activists ' fighting spirit . But it 's fair to wonder , in the wake of the Freedom Convoy , if this default strategy must be pursued more judiciously . <p> Dialogue and negotiation : Interim federal Conservative leader Candice Bergen has pressed the Trudeau government to extend " an olive branch " to the Freedom Convoy protesters -- to meet with them , discuss the situation , and work out a solution . That 's hard to do when the protesters ' manifesto demands the possible overthrow of said government . But talking things through is a time-honoured tradition in Canada . It 's why Trudeau urged " dialogue and mutual respect " to end the Indigenous rail blockades of 2020 , but there needs to be wiggle room @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Public opinion : Every protest is , in a way , a battle for hearts and minds -- on the streets , in the news , in council chambers and legislatures , and across social media . The more support a demonstration garners from ordinary Canadians , influencers , and decision-makers , the greater leverage its leaders have in negotiating a solution and achieving certain ends . At the same time , broad public support for a protest puts pressure on police and governments to tread more carefully in their response , and even to make concessions and compromises without seeming to capitulate to protesters ' demands . Conversely , a protest with little demonstrable public support can quickly run out of energy and resolve . That 's why the legitimizing support of the Freedom Convoy by some federal Conservatives has enraged local residents and drawn fire from the NDP and governing Liberals . <p> End-game strategy : Ultimately , all protests come to an end . If those involved do n't seem likely to return home voluntarily , a more or less forceful action by authorities will inevitably @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a dwindled number , if de-escalation has been successful -- and charging them with minor offences is a typical resolution . But it 's harder to imagine the Freedom Convoy wrapping up so easily , because of the hundreds of trucks -- many rigged to prevent towing -- currently blocking Wellington and other Ottawa streets . But , one way or another , a practical method is needed to bring any protest to a conclusion . And eventually , push will come to shove . <p> Rule of law : Those who object to anything but the mildest of protests will invoke the rule of law at the slightest misstep by activists . Chain yourself to a tree that is n't technically yours , and you can expect to be tossed in jail . Park your 18-wheeler in a no-stopping zone and expect expensive tickets , for a start , then the impounding of your vehicle and other legal consequences . The Freedom Convoy is proof that some mild law-breaking for a certain period of time will be tolerated by authorities ( and even the public ) in the name @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But patience eventually wears out ( note the class-action lawsuit facing the truckers , above ) . At the same time , respect for the rule of law is n't always called for . Just ask early-20th-century Franco-Ontarian mothers in Ottawa -- remembered today as heroines of the " Battle of the Hatpins " -- who clashed with police in January 1916 outside a Lowertown school and successfully defended their children 's rights to receive schooling in the French language . Guilbeault 's 2001 climb up the outside of the CN Tower during his years as a Greenpeace activist raises similar questions . In the 20 years since his illegal stunt , a global consensus has emerged that climate change is a real threat . Does that in any way excuse his dangerous law-breaking two decades ago ? <p> The consistency challenge : As the double-standard allegation of Alberta 's Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation makes clear , advocacy groups across Canada are closely watching police handling of the Freedom Convoy for signs that the truck protesters and their allies are being treated more tenderly than Indigenous activists and environmental protesters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pushing the Trudeau government to meet and negotiate with the truckers , in keeping with its guiding philosophy during the 2020 rail blockades . While every protest has unique features , it 's imperative that authorities strive to be as even-handed as possible -- and guided by consistent protocols -- in dealing with agitators from across the political spectrum and the disruptions caused by their actions . <p> The wild-card factor : Certain messages blared by the Freedom Convoy protesters -- such as a general fatigue with COVID restrictions -- will resonate with many Canadians . These are wild-card factors affecting the public perception of this protest , and many previous demonstrations in Canada have involved " rogue " actors , such as masked " antifa " infiltrators of various left-wing demonstrations . @@53638234 <p> Piles of sulfur in Vancouver , Canada . Experts say Canada 's low-carbon mining industry is in an ideal position to lead a global push to decarbonize.Pgiam / iStock / Getty Images Plus <p> The mining industry would see a financial windfall from a global carbon tax , so why does it keep fighting change ? That 's the contradiction researchers from the University of British Columbia examined in a study that has provoked strong opposition from the oil and gas industry . <p> The research , published in the journal Nature Communications Earth and Environment last week , provides evidence that , under a global carbon tax regime , mining companies would gain a competitive advantage over a variety of commodities across the fossil fuel industry , agriculture and construction . <p> At the best of times , the mining industry has remained fractured in its support of carbon tax schemes . Some companies have backed prices on carbon , while many industry organizations , like Minerals Council of Australia , have slammed carbon taxes as anti-job . <p> As a Mining Association of British Columbia advocacy paper echoed in October 2020 , the carbon tax is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mining . " <p> " The mining industry as a whole has this jerk reaction to carbon tax much like a meat-eater has a knee-jerk reaction going to a vegan restaurant , " said Cox , a PhD student at UBC 's Norman B. Keevil Institute of Mining Engineering . <p> " ' How dare you say we go there ? We do n't have anything to do with that . Those are n't our people . ' And what we 're trying to say is , ' Yes , the environmental movement , the pro-carbon-tax movement are your people . Get behind them . Support them . ' " <p> Cross-referencing public data on the carbon footprints and dollar value of 23 commodities -- from aluminum and copper to pork and cheese and coal and oil -- Cox and three other researchers have put a wrench in the narrative that all taxes are bad for business . <p> To make that transition to a low-carbon future , the mining of minerals like lithium , cobalt and rare earth metals are expected to skyrocket : the World Bank estimates more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ required to deploy enough wind , solar and other green technology to maintain global heating below the Paris Accord target of 2 C. <p> Today , the global mining and metals industry makes up eight per cent of humanity 's carbon footprint . But when comparing it to the fossil fuel or agricultural industry , the researchers found mining generated significantly more value for every tonne of emissions released into the atmosphere . <p> For every tonne of C02 produced in the mining of iron ore , for example , the industry generates US$9,400 . Those same emissions yield only about $250 worth of natural gas or $200 worth of cheese . <p> Perhaps most surprising , said Cox , the extraction and processing of metals like palladium and bauxite produce more than double the value the solar panel industry produces for every tonne of emissions . <h> HOW WOULD A GLOBAL CARBON TAX HELP ? <p> To date , more than 40 countries and over 30 sub-national jurisdictions have adopted some kind of carbon pricing . ( The Canadian government is planning to raise the federal carbon tax to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tonne by 2030 . ) <p> But that leaves over 150 nations without some form of carbon pricing -- a key financial mechanism experts say is working to drive economy-wide change . <p> Enter a global carbon tax . If it were set at $150 per tonne of carbon dioxide , the study found the cost would raise mining industry commodities between two and 30 per cent of their current value . By comparison , a similar global carbon tax would raise the cost of natural gas by 60 per cent , cement by 109 per cent , beef by 120 per cent and coal by 145 per cent . <p> Today , Cox says consumers end up choosing fossil fuel products or beef over their less carbon-intensive counterparts -- essentially because they are cheaper . But take carbon into account , and the balance would almost certainly tip in favour of products laced with commodities like copper , a key component in everything from wind turbines to electricity cables . <p> " From a GDP perspective , the mining industry has nothing to fear from carbon taxes because it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " said Cox . <p> There are some exceptions . <p> The manufacturing of steel requires both iron and coking coal -- the latter something the industry has yet to find a good substitution for at scale . So while a global carbon tax would n't directly impact iron mining operations , steel manufacturers and companies mining coking coal would be harder hit , and therefore will likely put up a bigger fight against a carbon tax , notes the study . <p> Producing aluminum , on the other hand , requires vast quantities of bauxite and energy . River Forecast Centre said this week some parts of the province are experiencing an elevated risk for spring melt-related flooding , although with months of snow accumulation left to go , things can change . <p> The Okanagan ( 90% ) , Boundary ( 88% ) and Similkameen ( 95% ) river basins are reporting snowpacks slightly below normal . The Lower Thompson ( 122% ) , North Thompson ( 118% ) and Middle Fraser ( 117% ) basins are sitting at above normal for this time of year . <p> " Seasonal weather forecasts from late January by Environment and Climate Change Canada indicate an increased likelihood of colder than normal temperatures from February through April for the entire province , " the River Forecast Centre says . <p> Forecasts from the CPC indicate a likelihood ( 67% chance ) of continued La Ni ? a conditions ( March-May 2022 ) , with a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spring 2022 ( April-June ) . <p> La Ni ? a occurs when oceanic temperature anomalies along the equatorial Pacific Ocean region are below normal for an extended period . <p> Historically , La Ni ? a conditions create cooler temperatures for British Columbia and wetter weather in the South Coast and Vancouver Island during the winter months . <p> By early February , nearly two-thirds of the annual B.C. snow pack has typically accumulated . <p> " The provincial average for all snow measurements across the province is 110% of normal and indicates a higher risk for snowmelt related flooding during the spring months ( freshet ) , particularly for the Interior , " said the River Forecast Centre . <p> " With a few months left for snow accumulation , seasonal snow packs can still change significantly . There are presently three rigs drilling in the Sa ? va sector testing areas to the northeast and west of the discovery area . Aggressive and methodical exploration of the sector is planned for 2022 as part of the $10 million exploration program at Chapada . Additional drill rigs and approximately fifty ( 50 ) holes are planned to test northeast along strike to towards the Formiga sector , as well as step out in other directions , as seen in Figure 2 . <p> Technical Information and Quality Assurance <p> The drill holes were collared at HQ diameter from soil to altered rock and changed to NQ when fresh @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ long and the wireline core drilling method was employed.The majority of holes were drilled at an azimuth of 120 ? and a 70 ? dip , perpendicular to interpreted strike and the mineralized horizon . However , some holes were drilled at other orientations where ideal surface access was not possible at the time . Downhole surveys were taken by the drilling contractor upon completion of the drill hole . All drill holes were surveyed every three ( 3 ) meters downhole using a Reflex GYRO SPRINT-IQ ? electronic surveying instrument . Generally , the deviation was below 5% , and no significant deviation issues were found to date . Collar surveys were taken by GPS with CenterPoint RTX in UTM coordinates , SAD 69 Brazil datum , 22 South Zone . Drill hole collars were cased and protected at the surface with a cement block affixed with a metal tag stamped with the drill hole number , final depth , inclination , azimuth , and start and finish dates . <p> All Lundin Mining assay results from drilling have been independently monitored through a quality assurance/quality control ( " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ standards , duplicates , blanks , and pulp and reject duplicate samples . The soil , saprolite , and altered rock were drilled from HQ size core and the fresh rock from NQ size core . Half of the core was collected , and the sample interval was around one ( 1 ) meter for mineralized zones and two ( 2 ) meters for non-mineralized zones . Quarter core samples were collected for duplicate analysis . The samples were securely transported by a locally based transport company from our core preparation facility at the Chapada Mine , Brazil to the ALS Chemex sample preparation facility in Goiania , Brazil . Sample pulps were sent for analysis to the same lab in Lima , Peru , which is independent of Lundin Mining . The samples were analyzed by fire assay/atomic absorption spectroscopy ( AAS ) ( gold ) and four acid digestion/ICP-MS ( copper ) . @@53638961 <h> The Power List <p> At the top of our annual Power List are the unknown victims of residential schools -- hundreds of children who lost their lives before they were finally heard . <p> Here , in brief , is the thinking behind our decision , which some may consider unorthodox . In 2021 , amid report after report of presumed grave sites being found on the former grounds of residential schools , non-Indigenous Canadians undeniably experienced an awakening . <p> Everyone from random citizens doing TV street interviews to the Prime Minister himself voiced horror and dismay , as if blindsided by the fact that the assimilationist project this country ran for the better part of a century had claimed the lives of children . Many , many children . <p> We were not blindsided , of course . The deaths of young Indigenous kids at places like Tk'eml ? ps , Cowessess and Williams Lake , B.C. were shared widely in the accounts of former students , who passed the knowledge to their children and grandchildren . They were meticulously reported by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 2015 . <p> We 've a long way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . But the massive shift in public attitudes that followed the grave discoveries is undeniable . Before making this choice , Maclean 's consulted privately with Indigenous , M ? t is and Inuit leaders , who unanimously approved of , and in some cases applauded , the idea . The grave finds , they agreed , changed the tone and substance of debate over Indigenous rights . Whether that change yields action , they 're waiting to see . <p> As in 2021 , our ranking hews toward good-faith actors pursuing positive change , even if their approaches , or their notions of positive , are not universally shared . Pierre Poilievre , the presumptive frontrunner for the leadership of the Conservative Party of Canada , is not everyone 's first choice as a seatmate on a long flight . But the Tory MP excels in his role as an opposition critic , holding the government 's feet to the fire . <p> And again , we 've looked beyond mere status . The nabobs of banking , lobbying , telecom and other arms of the establishment must do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ranking . <p> The result , we believe , is a list that reflects the pressing issues facing the country , and the opportunities ahead . Attentive readers will notice that Canadians who guided us through the first years of the pandemic -- public health leaders , epidemiologists -- have given way in this year 's ranking to those who will guide us out of it . <p> It 's our version of cautious optimism . With luck and good sense , we 'll emerge from Omicron into a world where COVID-19 is a managed risk , and we 'll refocus on the challenges that define Canada and its place in the world . As ever , our ability to navigate these problems will rest heavily on our brightest , bravest and most accomplished . Remember their names , and lend them your ears . <p> ( Amru Salahuddien/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images ) <p> 01 <h> The children who never came home <h> Indigenous affairs <p> A society deaf to their cries finally chooses to hear <p> In Secwepemcts ? n , the language of the Secw ? pemc , they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The ones taken to residential school who never returned . Survivors of Kamloops Indian Residential School in B.C. spoke of them , as did Elders across Canada who were forced into the notorious facilities . <p> In late May , Tk'eml ? ps te Secw ? pemc announced that some 200 presumed graves of le estcw ? ? had been found on the grounds of the Kamloops residential school . Waves of revulsion and guilt washed across the country . Through decades of testimony of abuse -- through the federal reports , legal settlements , formal apologies and a years-long public hashing-out of this national disgrace in the TRC -- there had been periodic outpourings of disgust and grief . But this shock was deeper , as non-Indigenous people and First Nations , M ? t is and Inuit alike thought of children 's lives being cut short while they attended these harsh , chronically underfunded and assimilation-focused boarding schools , and of hundreds being buried in something unthinkable in the non-Indigenous world : a school cemetery . <p> If this , to Canada 's discredit , is what it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ children will grow . @@53639619 <h> Europe 's Nuclear Fusion Race Is Going Private <p> The race is on to achieve commercial nuclear fusion . Believers in the " holy grail of clean energy " are hopeful that a breakthrough in nuclear fusion is imminent enough that the clean energy source could power a green energy transition sweeping and swift enough to help the world achieve the emissions targets set by the Paris climate accord . <p> In order to avoid the worst impacts of climate change , leading climate scientists and policymakers from around the world agree that the global community needs to keep the planet from warming more than 1.5 degrees Celcius over pre-industrial averages in the best-case scenario , and 2 degrees Celsius at worst . This is a tall order to say the least , considering past trends and a business-as-usual scenario , and will require unprecedented global cooperation and collaboration . What 's more , the window for achieving this kind of economic and systems overhaul is closing quickly . <p> Nuclear fusion has been posited as a kind of silver bullet solution to a seemingly insurmountable and wicked problem . For the better part of the last century @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ thought experiments rather than lab experiments . But in recent years major breakthroughs have brought commercial nuclear fusion closer to reality than ever before . Fusion , which is the form of energy production that powers the sun , involves the fusing of atoms , which emits several times more energy than nuclear fission , the atom-splitting technology that currently takes place at nuclear power plants . And , unlike nuclear fission , fusion leaves behind no radioactive waste and carries no risk of nuclear meltdown , making it an ideal candidate for a virtually limitless clean energy future . <p> So far , relatively few large-scale nuclear fusion initiatives have gotten off the ground , due to huge barriers to entry . Because of the enormous expense associated with building a reactor capable of facilitating fusion , so far the field has been dominated by publicly funded projects such as Europe 's ITER and China 's EAST ( Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak ) . As scientists have gotten closer and closer to achieving ' ignition ' -- which refers to a nuclear fusion reaction that emits more energy than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in getting into the industry on the bottom floor and positioning itself at the forefront of what could be a world-changing innovation . So far , while nuclear fusion has been successfully achieved in labs , ignition has remained elusive . <p> Now , however , the playing field is changing and competition is heating up as private enterprise gets involved . Last year , the nascent nuclear fusion sector was the recipient of more than 2.6 billion USD in venture capital , primarily in the United States . Now , however , fusion fever has hopped across the pond and is seriously gaining traction among private enterprises in Europe . Even in Germany , Europe 's preeminent anti-nuclear authority , nuclear fusion has gained significant ground . Marvel Fusion , a Munich-based company has raised 35 million Euros ( about 40 million USD ) for their nuclear fusion venture , and has recently solidified partnerships with Siemens Energy , France 's Thales , and the privately-owned German mechanical engineering group Trumpf . <p> Like some of its private counterparts in the United States , Marvel Fusion is not relying @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ basis of mass-scale fusion experiments like ITER , but is instead employing targeted lasters to trigger nuclear fusion reactions . This model is in its infancy , but holds great promise and has clearly gained the confidence of investors with deep pockets . " It 's a theoretical model , which is essentially a very large computer simulation , and then step by step it is being validated in an experimental campaign that started last year , " Marvel Fusion chief executive Moritz von der Linden told the Financial Times for an article published last week . <p> The newfound interest in nuclear fusion in Europe coincides with a serious energy crunch which has shown the fallibility of the continent 's energy security in recent months . The shortage of energy has sent energy prices through the roof and revealed the extent of Europe 's dependence on Russia for natural gas . The ability to create virtually limitless clean energy at will is an undeniably attractive possibility . With enough money and support from the public and private sectors across the world could give nuclear fusion the final push it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the planet from climate catastrophe and geopolitical crisis .

Macklem made a point of pushing back against arguments that his policies and fiscal stimulus were the main source of inflation . <p> " It is not the result of generalized excess demand in the Canadian economy , " Macklem said . " Our economy is only just now getting back to full capacity . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Macklem seems to think demand is n't the issue . @@53640891 <h> The risk of not talking to clients about ESG is losing them , RI expert says <p> This is the new Globe Advisor weekly newsletter for professional financial advisors , published every Friday . If someone has forwarded this newsletter to you via e-mail , or you 're reading this on the web , you can register for Globe Advisor , then sign up for this newsletter and others on our newsletter sign-up page . <p> Sustainable investing has become one of the fastest-growing investment themes in recent years as more people are paying closer attention to companies ' environmental , social , governance ( ESG ) performance . <p> Assets invested in sustainable mutual funds and exchange-traded funds ( ETFs ) roughly doubled to $34.5-billion in Canada at the end of 2021 , up from $17.4-billion a year earlier , according to a recent Morningstar Canada report . It also shows the industry launched 73 Canadian-based investment products last year , compared with 42 products the year prior . <p> " It 's a reflection of the growing interest that Canadians have for this area , " says Asmita Kanungo , national director , ESG practice management @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , which is focused on responsible investing ( RI ) . <p> The pandemic has changed how investors view RI and it 's expected to have a big impact on the registered retirement savings plan ( RRSP ) season currently underway , she says . <p> " The pandemic has highlighted many global inequalities including vaccine distribution , food insecurity and the lack of income support for those on sick leave , " Ms. Kanungo says . " Because these issues have been amplified , many people are now shifting the way they invest their money and which corporations they choose to support . " <p> Globe Advisor spoke with Ms. Kanungo about the rise in RI and how advisors can engage clients in this space : <p> What 's behind the rapid growth in RI in your view ? <p> Part of it is because our challenges are global in nature . Something like climate change does n't affect just one part of the world but the whole planet . It affects everyone . It 's highly visible . George Floyd 's murder became a catalyst for a more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ witnessed it . Climate change has been brought to life for all of us because we can see the fires burning . There 's a shift in investors ' values . There 's a trillion-dollar wealth transition from aging and predominantly male baby boomers to millennials and women -- two demographics that lean strongly toward aligning their values to the way they consume and invest . <p> How should advisors be engaging clients on RI ? <p> The Responsible Investment Association came out with an investor opinion survey last year showing that 77 per cent of investors would like their financial advisor to inform them about RI ; yet only 27 per cent of those investors indicated that their advisors are having that discussion . There 's what we call an ' RI service gap . ' Advisors need to be proactive about RI . It can be something as simple as asking a question like , ' What if you could achieve your financial goals while at the same time helping to improve society and the environment ? Is that something that would be interesting to you ? ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ program at NEI that helps advisors integrate RI within their practices . <p> What 's the risk of not talking to clients about ESG ? <p> I 've worked with hundreds of advisors across Canada to help them get comfortable and proactive in the space and , from what I 've heard , they 've never lost a client by bringing it up . In fact , they 've gained clients . However , some who have n't brought it up have said they 've lost clients . So , that 's a risk . Advisors do n't need to be experts in RI , but they should have a good understanding of the space and discussing it will only help to increase client engagement . 
@@53641096 <h> Toilet taboo : we need to stop being squeamish about recycling human waste <p> Clearly , toilets remain taboo . This has left many without toilets that can contain and treat waste safely or use large amounts of water to flush waste to energy-intensive , overloaded sewage networks and treatment works . ( File photo : Giorgio Trovato/Unsplash ) <p> When it comes to the humble toilet , most of us embrace a flush and forget approach that considers human excreta a waste product . But in a world experiencing climate change , this ignores the fact that organic waste can and must be recycled back into ecosystems . Despite their efficiency , toilets that recycle human waste are uncommon because most cultures consider them too unsavoury . <p> Many of the solutions to environmental challenges centre around new innovations and technologies . But what if it 's about more than that ? What if it 's more to do with culture , behaviour , learned taboos and prejudices ? <p> In our research we wanted to look at the idea of taboos around the subject and find out what might change people 's minds about technology that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ live and reduce their impact on the natural environment , the way we think about what is waste and what has value has to change . <h> Greener toilet technologies <p> Those in authority often make assumptions about what people will or wo n't accept -- without properly exploring how some technologies could be embraced . There has always been community resistance to wind farms , for example . This resistance is often dismissed by developers , when engagement with these communities can in fact lead to acceptance over time . Community ownership , where local people are involved and benefiting from the financial returns , can also increase acceptance . <p> Toilets which recycle human waste could significantly cut down on the amount of sewage that is currently overloading treatment works and convert the waste to an organic fertiliser and a clean fuel biogas . This can replace or reduce the use of traditional wood fuels , which cause indoor air pollution and related illnesses . <p> Domestic biogas technology enables toilets to be connected to an anaerobic digester -- airless units in which bacteria break down organic waste @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ common in low and middle-income countries but has the potential to be used more widely around the world . <h> Overcoming resistance <p> Toilet-linked anaerobic digesters ( TLADs ) have been met with a lot of resistance but there is surprisingly little information on how to allay fears and reservations or feelings of squeamishness about the technology . <p> In Nepal , despite cultural taboos that oppose the use of human waste products , there are reports of high numbers of TLADs . We wanted to see if we could learn something about how people came to accept them . Conducting in-depth interviews with rural householders we questioned them about cultural and religious objections around purity and pollution and how they were renegotiated to allow adoption of TLADs . <p> Most importantly , we found that time was needed for social norms to change and for initial feelings of resistance to be overcome . In some instances , households only installed TLADs after the older generations , who were more opposed to the technology , had passed away . <p> Community leaders -- or as we called them " risk @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the anerobic digester toilets . Risk-takers were people who installed TLADs even when the rest of the community did not approve . Some worried TLADs would make their home smell , or be unhygienic , but once they were able to see one at work , they realised that was n't the case . <p> Further benefits , such as free cooking fuel which dispensed with the need to find firewood , and the absence of smoke inside the home , plus better toilet design and fewer disposal issues convinced people of the technology 's usefulness . Demonstrations by neighbours and opportunities to learn how TLADs worked were successful in encouraging people to install their own . <p> How biogas and fertiliser are produced in a Nepali household with an anaerobic digester.Natalie Boyd Williams/University of Stirling , Author provided <h> Embracing the future <p> From our findings it is clear that policymakers should not base decisions on the public 's initial perceptions about recycling toilets . They need to win people over by demonstrating the technologies and explaining the benefits to themselves and the environment . And they must @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ idea and get beyond their discomfort with practices they find challenging . <p> In the community we studied in Nepal , most people adopted TLADs when it was more socially acceptable to do so . In Singapore where drinking water from recycled sewage is widely accepted , authorities promoted positive media campaigns that communicated the science and environmental value , but more importantly , made consuming recycled water utterly normal . Policymakers should recognise the power of social norms and the positive as well as negative role the media can play in communicating information . <p> This study can also teach us something about our own resistance towards recycling . In the UK , sewage and food waste is converted into biogas and agricultural fertiliser using anaerobic digestion on an industrial scale -- but smaller scale biogas units remain futuristic . We need to go beyond initial reactions of reluctance and squeamishness to understand how change can happen when we have the proper information , when we can see demonstrable benefits and when we can contribute to improving the environment .

@@53641290 <h> Durable water repellent , the devil of the outdoor equipment industry <p> Research indicates that the chemicals used to make waterproof clothes are toxic . COURTESY OF OLIVIA BASILE UNSPLASH <p> What do waterproof running shoes , a non-stick pan , and your rain jacket have in common ? Do n't Google it , because I 'll answer it for you here : DWR . <p> If you have ever gotten lost in an outdoor equipment store , you 've probably heard the acronym ' DWR ' thrown around once or twice -- but what does it really mean ? ' DWR ' stands for ' durable water repellent , ' and it 's the umbrella term for a host of active ingredients in your waterproof gear that produces that classic beading effect on the surface of your gear that keeps you dry . Teflon , Gore-Tex and Pertex -- some other terms you might have heard while shopping that sent your mind spinning -- are patented forms of DWR . <p> DWR and its patented recipes are composed of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAs ) . PFAs appear in the bloodstream of 98.5 per cent of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they last so long in the environment . They 're also found in many common products . <p> You will see outdoor companies use the term ' perfluorocarbons ' ( PFCs ) instead of ' PFAs , ' and while that is n't necessarily wrong , it is misleading . PFAs are a large class of 4,700 harmful chemicals used in firefighting foam , waterproof carpeting , snack packaging , and DWR . The distinction is important to note because although outdoor gear companies still talk about them , PFCs were a subset of chemicals banned in the 1980s because they were eating up the ozone layer . As a rule of thumb , when you hear an outdoor company say PFCs , think PFAs . <p> PFAs are compounds with a hydrophilic ' head ' made from oxygen and hydrogen and a hydrophobic ' tail ' made from carbon and fluorine . They are notoriously difficult to break down , and have one of the strongest bonds known in organic chemistry . <p> How do they work ? <p> The reason that PFAs work so well is that they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hring , a chemistry professor at Ryerson University who researches them . <p> " Normally , when you have a chemical , it 's either hydrophilic or hydrophobic . So it either loves water , or it hates water , " S ? hring explained in an interview with The Varsity . A chemical usually ca n't have both characteristics , and PFAs are unique because they do . " That is why it 's so loved in outdoor clothing , because it repels dirt and it repels water , " said S ? hring . <p> Not only do PFAs have a unique half-hydrophilic and half-hydrophobic chemistry , but they 're durable too . The half lives of PFAs vary from months to years , which makes them persistent and bioaccumulative , meaning we absorb them faster than we can get them to leave our bodies . The longer the compound 's ' tail , ' the longer the chemical 's life . This is why , for decades , the outdoor industry used longer-chain carbons like C8 -- a chain of eight carbon atoms in a bond . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to move away from these long-chain carbons . Why ? Because of their toxicity . <p> And they 're more than carcinogenic ; PFAs have filled up quite the rap sheet . In 2009 , the EPA described them as " persistent , bioaccumulative , and toxic " and research has since found a link between PFA exposure and a long list of health defects , such as certain forms of cancer , pregnancy and fertility problems , hormone disruptions , delayed puberty , and bone density changes , to name a few . <p> It is also important to keep in mind that PFAs remain critically under-researched . Therefore , we do n't know the effects of every kind of PFA , let alone what they could do in combination . " We have like 5000 PFAs , and we 've analyzed maybe 80 , 100 , if you 're really good , " S ? hring said . These low rates , she pointed out , are happening in an era where PFAs research is " definitely taking off . " <p> To avoid bioaccumulation , chemists shorten @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tail . Starting in the 2010s , there has been a move away from C8s within the outdoor industry . Although a few companies even offer PFC-free options , such as Columbia 's ExtremeEco jacket , the majority have opted for C6 or C4 chains . Recently , massive companies like MEC , Patagonia , Arc'teryx and Gore-Tex have released press statements that favour short-chain compounds . <p> But are shorter chain PFAs any less toxic ? " For all intents and purposes , no , " said S ? hring . She explained that PFAs with a lower chain length tend to be more water soluble than their longer chain counterparts . " That just means that the lower chain PFAs are more of a drinking water problem rather than a food problem , " S ? hring added . <p> Instead of being bioaccumulative , short chain PFAs are mobile . According to Amila De Silva of Environment Canada , PFAs can even be found in snow collected from " the cleanest place on Earth . " Because of these mobile short-chain PFAs , there has been a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and toxic " chemicals along with the " persistent , bioaccumulative , toxic " category . <p> It 's here that the problem with the outdoor industry 's waterproof gear reaches its crux : the gear the industry provides actively violates the community 's ' Leave No Trace ' policy on an insidious , molecular level . <p> But they have new investors to think about , who may have different priorities . There are alternative forms of DWR , like NikWax , that can be used to create waterproof gear -- but their lifespan depends on consumer maintenance . This begs the question : will today 's outdoors community retain the environmentalism of its self-ratified hippie hiker and climbing-trash founders ? Or will it follow the lead of the executives with commercial interests and find a way to internally justify the environmental cost ? <p> So far , the magnates of the outdoors industry have n't willingly met the challenge . PFAs still do not have proper regulation in Canada . It 's up to Health Canada and Environment and Climate Change Canada to assess if a new product @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ three months . The regulation is clearly exploitable and the industry knows it . <p> For the North American consumer it 's even worse -- not only do the provided options degrade the realm you aim to venture into and stay safe in , but it can feel like there 's little to no way to make an informed choice . It is unfair to put the onus on the consumer , but it 's important to make responsible purchasing decisions ; in North America , you " vote with your money , " as the saying goes . <p> I do n't expect you to be or feel responsible for what is happening . The least I can do is offer you resources , though , because in a climate that makes an informed decision difficult , you at least deserve to be able to try .
